title: The Visitation (31 May)
hook: May ends where Mary's traveling began, with Elizabeth

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mary, Help of Christians, the guest at Cana who noticed the wine was gone. Your line was help of Christians.

A young woman has just heard news that will change everything. An angel, Luke says, has told her she will bear a son. In the same breath, the angel mentions her older relative Elizabeth, who was called barren, and who is now with child too. What does she do next? She doesn't sit at home with the secret. She doesn't wait to be sure. She packs and goes, up into the hill country, to the one other woman who might understand. Today, the last feast of May: the Visitation.
screen: `NEWS THAT CHANGES EVERYTHING.` → `ELIZABETH IS WITH CHILD TOO.` → `SHE PACKS AND GOES.`

segments.voice: Here's how Luke puts it, in the Douay-Rheims: "And Mary rising up in those days, went into the hill country with haste into a city of Juda." With haste. Mary doesn't drift. She goes. Then the arrival. Mary greets Elizabeth, and Luke says the child in Elizabeth's womb leaps. Elizabeth, filled with the Holy Spirit, cries out with a loud voice: "Blessed art thou among women, and blessed is the fruit of thy womb." Those words may sound familiar. Catholics say them in the Hail Mary, after the angel's greeting, so they pray this meeting every time they say it. Notice who is in the room. Two women, one old and one young, both carrying children nobody expected. No priests, no crowds, no kings. Two relatives in a house in the hills, and the one Luke says leaped for joy is a child not yet born. Then Mary answers with a song of her own, the one Catholics call the Magnificat and still sing at evening prayer. And she stays: about three months, Luke says. Not a quick visit and a gift at the door. Luke doesn't say what filled those months; tradition pictures her helping as Elizabeth's time drew near. That's the shape of the feast. Good news doesn't make Mary sit still. It sends her out, fast, to someone who needs company, and once she's there, she doesn't hurry away.
screen: `MARY GOES WITH HASTE.` · `THE CHILD LEAPS.` · `BLESSED ART THOU AMONG WOMEN.` · `SHE STAYS ABOUT THREE MONTHS.` · then, large: `SHE WENT IN HASTE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who might need company right now: someone expecting a child or caring for one, someone older living alone, someone carrying news they haven't told many people. Notice what has kept you from going, waiting for a better week or for the right words, and picture the soonest real moment you could be with them, phone away, no glance at the clock. If you pray, say Elizabeth's words, the ones Catholics say in the Hail Mary; if you don't, simply hold that person in mind.
The Visitation. Mary's journey into the hill country to visit Elizabeth, where the child leaped and Elizabeth called her blessed.
Your line: she went in haste. Quick to arrive, and in no hurry to leave. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of the Visitation on 31 May, closing the month Catholic tradition dedicates to Mary; Elizabeth's greeting is prayed in every Hail Mary, and the Magnificat is sung at Evening Prayer.

fork.setup: you're Mary. an angel has just told you your news, and that your relative Elizabeth is expecting too. what do you do?

write to Elizabeth when you're ready.
set out at once for the hill country.

original.note: Greek, Luke 1:39: with haste — also with eagerness, earnestness.

chat.says: What is the Visitation that Catholics celebrate at the end of May?
options: Mary hurrying to visit Elizabeth, whose child leaped, and staying about three months.
The angel Gabriel's visit to Mary to tell her she would bear a son.
The Magi visiting the newborn Jesus with gold, frankincense and myrrh.
chat.meaning: The feast remembers Mary going in haste to Elizabeth: the child leaps, Elizabeth calls her blessed, and Mary stays about three months.

Elizabeth.meaning: Mary's older relative, with child in her old age

Juda.meaning: the region of the hill country Mary traveled to

Magnificat.meaning: Mary's song of praise in Luke's Gospel

Hail Mary.meaning: a Catholic prayer using the angel's and Elizabeth's words

notes: Confirm Douay-Rheims wording of Luke 1:39 and 1:42 exactly.
'About three months' (Luke 1:56) is from the cited text.
'The first person to recognize Jesus is a child not yet born': an interpretive reading of 1:41–44; consider 'some readers say'.
Hail Mary: first half joins Luke 1:28 and 1:42; 'became the first half' stated as fact. Confirm.
Magnificat sung at Evening Prayer (Vespers) daily in the Liturgy of the Hours; confirm wording 'every evening in the Church's prayer'.
howItsDone: 'many parishes dedicate' May to Mary; confirm or soften.
Greek μετὰ σπουδῆς: sense of haste/earnestness per lexicons; confirm note and pronunciation.
End of May: close points to June (Kevin of Glendalough).

Editor: cut the superlative 'the first person to recognize Jesus' (now the child who leaps for joy, per Luke 1:44) and the invented kitchen; cut the Greek-meaning aside (day 987 already used a Greek-word angle); softened 'every evening' and 'many parishes'; rewrote the practice, which repeated day 977's planned-visit practice (door, what to bring), to focus on going soon and staying.

Audit: 'she stays long enough to help' stated as Luke's text; Luke 1:56 gives only the length of the stay, so it is now marked as tradition. 'Leaps for joy at Jesus' (an interpretation) now follows Luke 1:44's wording. DR Luke 1:39 and 1:42 checked.
